SUBJECT:      PALISADES NUCLEAR PLANT – ISSUANCE OF AMENDMENT NO. 283
              REGARDING MODIFICATION OF THE LICENSING BASIS TO ALLOW
              ALTERNATIVE FUEL HANDLING METHOD FOR THE RECOVERY OF FUEL
              ASSEMBLY DD41 (EPID L-2026-LLA-0201) (EXIGENT CIRCUMSTANCES)

Dear Sir or Madam:

The U.S. Nuclear Regulatory Commission (the Commission) has issued the enclosed
Amendment No. 283 to Renewed Facility Operating License No. DPR-20 for the Palisades
Nuclear Plant. The amendment consists of changes to the license basis in response to your
application dated September 30, 2026, as supplemented by letters dated October 2, 2026,
October 8, 2026, and October 12, 2026.

The amendment revises the Updated Final Safety Analysis Report to allow for the removal of
the DD41 fuel assembly from the reactor cavity and move the assembly to the spent fuel pool.

This amendment is issued under exigent circumstances as provided in the provisions of
paragraph 50.91(a)(6) of Title 10 of the Code of Federal Regulations due to the time-critical
nature of the amendment. In this instance, an exigent situation exists in that the amendment is
needed to allow movement of the fuel assembly out of the reactor cavity in order to resume
loading fuel and move toward reactor startup.

A copy of our related safety evaluation is also enclosed. The safety evaluation describes the
exigent circumstances under which the amendment was issued and the NRC staff’s final no
significant hazards determination.
                                              -2-


The Notice of Issuance and opportunity for a hearing associated with the exigent circumstances
will be included in a future biweekly Federal Register notice.

                                           Sincerely,


                                           /RA/

                                           Justin C. Poole, Senior Project Manager
                                           Operating Reactor Licensing Branch 3
                                           Division of Licensing Projects 1
                                           Office of Nuclear Reactor Regulation

       SAFETY EVALUATION BY THE OFFICE OF NUCLEAR REACTOR REGULATION

                            RELATED TO AMENDMENT NO. 283 TO

                  RENEWED FACILITY OPERATING LICENSE NO. DPR-20

                                  HOLTEC PALISADES, LLC.

                                  PALISADES ENERGY, LLC

                                PALISADES NUCLEAR PLANT

                                      DOCKET NO. 50-255



1.0    INTRODUCTION

By letter dated September 30, 2026 (Agencywide Documents Access and Management System
(ADAMS) Accession Nos. ML26273A469), as supplemented by letters dated October 2, 2026,
October 8, 2026, and October 12, 2026 (ML26275A214, ML26281A333, and ML26285A034,
respectively), to the U.S. Nuclear Regulatory Commission (NRC or the Commission), Palisades
Energy, LLC (the licensee), submitted a license amendment request (LAR) to make certain
changes to the Renewed Facility Operating License DPR-20 for Palisades Nuclear Plant
(Palisades, PNP).

The proposed amendment would modify the PNP Updated Final Safety Analysis Report
(UFSAR) to allow for the removal of the DD41 fuel assembly from the reactor cavity and move
the assembly to the spent fuel pool using an alternative process. Specifically, the proposed
amendment would modify UFSAR sections 9.11 and 14.19, on a one-time basis, to describe an
alternative fuel-handling process. While the licensee requested approval of the proposed
change as an emergency license amendment in accordance with the regulations at Title 10 of
the Code of Federal Regulations (10 CFR) 50.91(a)(5), the NRC processed this amendment
request as an exigent amendment in accordance with 10 CFR 50.91(a)(6).

2.0    REGULATORY EVALUATION

2.1    System Description

Section 9.11 of the PNP UFSAR describes the operation and requirements of the fuel handling
and storage system for new and spent fuel. This section of the UFSAR contains descriptions of
the structural analysis of the Spent Fuel Pool (SFP) and criticality prevention analysis, as well
as descriptions of the new fuel storage areas. Section 14.19 of the PNP UFSAR describes the
possibility of an accident with significant consequences during refueling. For the purpose of



                                                                                      Enclosure 2
                                                 -2-


defining the upper limit of the radiological consequences of a fuel handling accident, it is
assumed that the fuel bundle is dropped during handling.

2.2    Licensee’s Proposed Changes

PNP has proposed revisions to UFSAR sections 9.11 and 14.19 to describe an alternative fuel-
handling process. The process would be a one-time operation limited to recovery of fuel
assembly DD41. Once recovery of fuel assembly DD41 is completed, PNP plans to transition
the changes to historical UFSAR content. As stated in Section 2.3 of the LAR, below is a
description of the proposed revisions:

       The alternative fuel-handling process would lift DD41 using the Containment
       Polar Crane (L-1) and purpose-designed fuel movement device (FMD) supported
       by slings and chain-falls to remove the assembly from the reactor. Once removed
       from the reactor, DD41 would be loaded underwater into the FTC [Fuel Transfer
       Canister] staged on the reactor cavity floor. The FTC containing DD41 would be
       lifted from the water, drained, and then transported through containment using
       the crane and existing rail system along a lift path that exits through the
       containment equipment hatch into the SFP area of the auxiliary building. Once in
       the SFP area, the FTC would be lifted using the Fuel Pool Building Crane (L-3)
       and placed vertically in the Region 2 cask laydown area of the SFP.

       All existing radiation protection analyses, heavy-load lift analyses, and
       procedures have been reviewed and revised, as necessary, to incorporate
       requirements associated with this lift. These changes would be incorporated into
       the applicable procedures before any fuel-handling activity using the alternative
       process.

2.3    Regulatory Requirements and Guidance

The regulatory requirements and guidance on which the NRC based its acceptance and
evaluation of this LAR are listed below.

Regulatory Requirements

PNP was designed prior to the publishing of the Atomic Energy Commission (AEC) “General
Design Criteria (GDC) for Nuclear Power Plant Construction Permits,” draft for comment,
32 FR 10214 (July 1967). Therefore, PNP was not licensed to the current 10 CFR Part 50,
Appendix A, GDC. The PNP principal design criteria for the design, construction, and operation
of the plant are listed in PNP UFSAR, section 1.4, “Principal Design Criteria.” An evaluation
comparing the PNP design basis to the AEC GDCs as they appeared in 10 CFR Part 50,
Appendix A on July 7, 1971, is presented in PNP UFSAR, section 5.1, “General Design
Criteria.” The portions of the UFSAR applicable to this amendment include GDC 61, “Fuel
storage and handling and radioactivity control,” and PNP UFSAR sections 1.4.8 “RADIOACTIVE
WASTES AND RADIATION PROTECTION” and 1.4.9 “FUEL HANDLING AND STORAGE”.
UFSAR section 1.4.8 states:

       The radioactive waste treatment system was designed so that discharge of
       radioactivity to the environment is in accordance with the requirements of 10
       CFR, Part 20, and Appendix I to 10 CFR 50. The Facility was provided with a
       centralized control room having adequate shielding to permit occupancy during
                                                -3-


       all credible accident situations. The radiation shielding in the Facility, in
       combination with Facility radiation control procedures, ensures that personnel do
       not receive radiation exposures in excess of the applicable limits of 10 CFR, Part
       20, during normal evolutions and maintenance.

UFSAR section 1.4.9 states: “Fuel handling and storage facilities were provided for the safe
handling, storage and shipment of fuel and will preclude accidental criticality.”

Section 50.67, “Accident source term,” of 10 CFR states that any licensee that was initially
authorized to operate prior to January 10, 1997, and who seeks to revise the current accident
source term in its design basis radiological consequence analyses, must apply for a license
amendment under 10 CFR 50.90, “Application for amendment or license, construction permit, or
early site permit.” Paragraph (b)(2) of 10 CFR 50.67 provides that the NRC may issue the
amendment if the application’s analysis demonstrates with reasonable assurances the following:
   (i)      An individual located at any point on the boundary of the exclusion area for any
            2-hour period following the onset of the postulated fission product release, would not
            receive a radiation dose in excess of 0.25 Sv [Sievert] (25 rem [roentgen equivalent
            man]) total effective dose equivalent (TEDE).
   (ii)     An individual located at any point on the outer boundary of the low population zone,
            who is exposed to the radioactive cloud resulting from the postulated fission product
            release (during the entire period of its passage), would not receive a radiation dose in
            excess of 0.25 Sv (25 rem) total effective dose equivalent (TEDE), and
   (iii)    Adequate radiation protection is provided to permit access to ad occupancy of the
            control room under accident conditions without personnel receiving radiation
            exposures in excess of 0.05 Sv (5 rem) total effective dose equivalent (TEDE) for the
            duration of the accident.

Additionally, under Section 50.92(a) of 10 CFR, in determining whether an amendment to a
license will be issued, the NRC staff is guided by the considerations that govern the issuance of
initial licenses to the extent applicable and appropriate. The common standards for licenses in
10 CFR 50.40(a), and those specifically for issuance of operating licenses in 10 CFR
50.57(a)(3), provide that there must be “reasonable assurance” that the activities at issue will
not endanger the health and safety of the public, and that the applicant will comply with the
Commission’s regulations.

Guidance Documents

      NUREG-0612, “Control of Heavy Loads at Nuclear Power Plants: Resolution of Generic
       Technical Activity A-36,” July 1980.
      NUREG-0800, Section 15.0.3, “Design Basis Accident Radiological Consequence
       Analyses for Advanced Light Water Reactors,” March 2007.
      NUREG-0800, Section 15.7.4, “Radiological Consequences of Fuel Handling Accidents,”
       July 1981.
      NUREG-1565, “Dry Oxidation and Fracture of LWR Spent Fuels,” November 1996.
      Regulatory Guide (RG) 1.183, Revision 0, “Alternative Radiological Source Terms for
       Evaluating Design Basis Accidents at Nuclear Power Reactors,” July 2000.
      Interim Staff Guidance (ISG)-11, “Cladding Considerations for the Transportation and
       Storage of Spent Fuel,” Revision 3.
      NUREG-2216, “Standard Review Plan for Transportation Packages for Spent Fuel and
       Radioactive Material.”
                                                 -4-


         NUREG-2215, “Standard Review Plan for Spent Fuel Dry Storage Systems and
          Facilities.”

3.0       TECHNICAL EVALUATION

The NRC staff reviewed the LAR to determine if the proposed revisions to the UFSAR meet the
requirements in section 2.3 above.

3.1       Change to UFSAR Section 9.11, Fuel Handling and Storage Systems

The licensee has proposed a one-time change to UFSAR section 9.11.4 to define an alternate
fuel handling method using a FTC and a Fuel Handling Device.

UFSAR section 9.11.4 defines the normal handling of fuel assemblies during fuel loading.
Normally the refueling machine removes a spent fuel assembly from the core, transports it to
the tilt machine, and deposits it in the transfer carriage within the tilt machine. The carriage is
then rotated from a vertical position to a horizontal position and moved through the transfer tube
to the spent fuel storage area. The carriage is then rotated to a vertical position, the spent fuel
removed and placed in a storage rack by the service platform. Due to the conditions described
in the LAR, fuel assembly DD41 cannot be recovered using the refueling machine or transfer
tube as the method described in UFSAR, and the licensee has proposed an alternative method.

The alternative transfer process described in the LAR consists of using the Containment Polar
Crane (L-1) to transfer DD41 into the laydown area within the reactor cavity. To minimize risk
while moving fuel within the reactor cavity, the licensee developed a specially designed fuel
movement device (FMD) to move fuel assembly to the FTC. DD41 is currently oriented at an
approximate 30-degree angle with the lower tie plate in core location H-1 and the upper tie plate
leaning against the core shroud on the opposite side of the core. Fuel assembly DD41 will be
maintained at a minimum of 10 feet underwater while being lifted and transferred to the FTC
within reactor cavity. This FTC encloses the fuel assembly to enable lifting out of the reactor
cavity. The fuel will be laid down into the FTC horizontally and an FTC cover installed. During
the operation, the radiological consequences of fuel handling accident (FHA) with assembly
DD41 within the reactor cavity under the assumed 10 feet of water or when placed in the spent
fuel pool, remain bounded by the existing FHA described in UFSAR section 14.19.

Once the fuel assembly and lid are secured on the FTC, the canister is lifted out of water using
the Containment Polar Crane (L-1), drained, and moved to the equipment hatch location where
it is placed on an equipment hatch trolley for transfer to the SFP within auxiliary building. As
indicated by licensee, the FTC is handled along established safe load path using developed
procedures. To minimize consequence of accident, the licensee has performed a load drop
analysis. The review of the FTC Drop Analysis is covered below in section 3.4 Recovery
Equipment – Drop Analysis.

Within the auxiliary building, a single failure proof fuel handling crane is used to lift the FTC and
rotate into vertical configuration to lower into the cask pit located within the spent fuel pool. The
licensee has taken safety precautions, including use of single failure proof crane and
administrative controls, to minimize risk while rotating and lowering the FTC into the SFP. The
licensee has further described the loaded FTC movements within the fuel building following a
procedurally established safe load path. In letter dated October 8, 2026, the licensee’s response
to the Request for Additional Information (RAI) verified that the L-3 fuel building crane is
                                                 -5-


currently configured as single failure proof from previously supporting the last dry fuel loading
campaign and will retain the single failure proof configuration while handling DD41 and FTC.

The assembled and loaded FTC has an approximate lift weight of 49,000 pounds. Based on
weight, the loads moved during the alternative method are considered heavy loads.
NUREG-0612 provides criteria for control of heavy loads. If a heavy load were to drop, they
could impact on stored spent fuel, fuel in the core, or equipment that may be required to achieve
safe shutdown or permit continued decay heat removal. General criteria for programmatic
guidelines for design, operation, testing, maintenance, and inspection are specified in
NUREG-0612, including safe load paths and procedures which have been developed. As
described, the licensee has evaluated handling fuel assembly from reactor cavity to spent fuel
pool and developed corresponding procedures for safe handling utilizing the proposed
alternative transfer process. The staff has accessed and considered the licensee-provided fuel
handling procedure (FHSO-19A) on their electronic portal to gain an understanding of the
process.

Based on the alternative recovery process described in the LAR for this one-time handling of
fuel assembly relocation, the staff finds adequate description is provided in updated UFSAR
9.11.4 for safe handling of fuel and minimizing risk of a dropped load.

3.2     Fuel Handling Accident

3.2.1   Change to Fuel Handling Accident

A fuel handling accident is considered a design bases accident at Palisades that requires a
radiological consequences analysis. As documented in PNP UFSAR section 14.11, “Postulated
Cask Drop Accidents,” and section 14.19, “Fuel Handling Accident,” this analysis was previously
performed to comply with Regulatory Guide (RG) 1.183, Revision 0 “Alternative Radiological
Source Terms for Evaluating Design Basis Accidents at Nuclear Power Reactors.” RG 1.183
outlines various assumptions and methodologies the staff find acceptable for performing the
radiological consequence analysis. Appendix B of RG 1.183 details assumptions for evaluating
the radiological consequences of an FHA. HI-2261348, Revision 1 “Radiological Consequences
of DD41 FHA at Palisades” – which documents the analysis performed in alignment with RG
1.183 – was included as an attachment to the LAR.

Based on previous radiological consequence analyses, an FHA was assumed to occur using
equipment that was dedicated to fuel handling (such as the fuel handling manipulator crane).
Additionally, all fuel movement during refueling operations was assumed to occur under water
with a minimum depth of 23 ft of water on top of the assembly in either the containment
refueling cavity or spent fuel pool. The water in the cavity and the pool during fuel movement
supports the radiological consequence analyses because it provides shielding to workers, and
during a hypothetical FHA the water retains some of the fission products that are released.

The staff evaluated the proposed movement of fuel assembly DD41 since the licensee
proposed a new proposed pathway out of containment to the spent fuel pool. The proposed use
of the polar crane (as opposed to the fuel manipulator crane) enables PNP to move fuel directly
out of the refueling cavity (and water). The licensee’s plan is to place DD41 in an engineered
Fuel Transfer Canister (FTC) and then take the FTC, with DD41 within it, out of the water. The
planned removal pathway takes the FTC out of containment through an equipment hatch, so
any mitigation of an FHA accident dose consequence analysis from water in the refueling cavity
or SFP cannot be credited.
                                                 -6-


3.2.2   Source Term

The fission product inventory that constitutes the source term for this event is the gap activity in
the fuel rods assumed to be damaged because of the postulated design basis FHA. Volatile
constituents of the core fission product inventory migrate from the fuel pellets to the gap
between the pellets and the fuel rod cladding during normal power operations. The fission
product inventory in the fuel rod gap of the damaged fuel rods is assumed to be instantaneously
released because of the accident.

The source term for the Palisades DD41 FHA was developed in accordance with NRC
Regulatory Guide 1.183, Appendix B, which prescribes conservative assumptions for accident
radiological consequence analyses. The inventory of radionuclides considered for release was
derived from the calculated isotopic data for fuel assembly DD41. Only those nuclides residing
in the fuel rod gap and plenum (specifically noble gases, halogens, and alkali metals) were
included in the FHA analysis, consistent with regulatory position 1.2 of RG 1.183, Appendix B.
For an FHA in containment, no source term was considered for fuel assemblies other than
DD41.

A key conservative assumption in the source term modeling is the extent of fuel damage. The
analysis assumes that all fuel rods in DD41 are damaged and their entire gap inventory is
available for release. This aligns with Regulatory Guide 1.183, Appendix B regulatory
position 1.1. The total inventory is then modified in the RADTRAD code by applying
radionuclide-specific release fractions and timings provided in RG 1.183. For FHA, all gap
activity is assumed to be released instantaneously further ensuring conservatism in the dose
calculations.

Consistent with regulatory position 1.3 of RG 1.183, Appendix B, the analysis assumes that
iodine is released as 95 percent cesium iodide (CsI), 4.85 percent elemental iodine, and 0.15
percent organic iodide. These fractions are applied to the gap inventory of iodine isotopes,
reflecting the expected speciation under accident conditions. The release fractions for other
radionuclide groups are also taken directly from Table 3 of RG 1.183. The source term is thus
constructed to represent a worst-case, yet realistic, scenario modeling the FHA.

The resulting source term is processed through the RADTRAD model, which simulates
transport, and mitigation of radioactive material through plant compartments and release
pathways. The model accounts for the effects of filtration (e.g., HEPA and charcoal filters in the
fuel handling building (FHB) stack exhaust), atmospheric dispersion, and receptor
characteristics (breathing rates, occupancy factors). The NRC staff finds that the source term
developed for PNP DD41 FHA was generated in accordance with RG 1.183, Revision 0.

3.2.3   Transport

The transport pathways evaluated in this FHA differ substantially from those in a standard
fuel‑handling accident because the proposed recovery method removes the irradiated fuel
assembly from its normal underwater shielding environment and carries it above water within an
engineered FTC. In a typical FHA, radionuclides released from damaged rods are assumed to
be instantaneously mixed within the surrounding water of the refueling cavity or spent fuel pool,
where significant mitigation occurs through water holdup and large decontamination factors are
credited under RG 1.183. By contrast, the Palisades DD41 recovery introduces periods during
which the assembly is transported dry, first when the FTC is lifted from the reactor cavity, then
as it travels across containment, through the open containment equipment hatch, and into the
                                                -7-


FHB. Because these steps occur outside a water environment, none of the standard FHA
water‑scrubbing or iodine retention mechanisms can be credited. As a result, the bounding
radiological transport scenario assumes direct atmospheric mixing within containment,
unmitigated flow through the open equipment hatch into the FHB, and subsequent exhaust
through the FHB ventilation and filtration system to the plant stack, representing a more
conservative, and fundamentally distinct transport configuration than the conventional
underwater FHA pathway.

A critical component of the transport evaluation is the configuration of the containment
equipment hatch. The applicant assumes the hatch is open at the time of the postulated drop–a
configuration explicitly chosen because it maximizes potential release to adjacent plant areas
and results in higher offsite and control room dose consequences. With the hatch open,
radionuclides in the containment atmosphere are transported directly into the FHB with no credit
for holdup or deposition in containment during the transfer. These assumptions bound accident
transport modeling during the fuel‑handling in containment.

Once radionuclides enter the FHB, transport is governed by the building’s engineered ventilation
system, which exhausts through a high‑capacity filtration train to the plant stack. The applicant
modeled the FHB exhaust at 75,000 cubic feet per minute (cfm) and credited filtration
efficiencies of 99 percent for aerosols and 94 percent for elemental and organic iodine. The
transport model does not take credit for deposition on surfaces, leakage into adjacent plant
spaces, or additional building holdup, ensuring that the filtered stack exhaust pathway is the
sole mechanism by which radionuclides leave the building.

Transport to the control room was modeled using both unfiltered and filtered intake streams,
reflecting transitions between normal, and emergency ventilation modes. Prior to control room
isolation, the model applies an unfiltered intake of 660 cfm, allowing a portion of airborne
material to enter the control room without removal. At 20 minutes, consistent with the applicant’s
credited operator action, the control room shifts to emergency mode, eliminating unfiltered
intake, and initiating filtered make-up and recirculation flows providing 99 percent removal
efficiency for aerosols, elemental iodine, and organic iodine. The control room model also
incorporates unfiltered in‑leakage of 100 cfm.

Initially, it was not clear to the staff if the movement of DD41 in the FHB was considered by the
licensee or bounded by their radiological consequence analysis in HI-2261348, Revision 1
(ML26273A469). As stated in the supplement to the LAR dated October 2, 2026 – the planned
travel path of DD41 (in the FTC) would be “over the North Tilt Pit where spent fuel is currently
stored.” HI-2261348, Rev. 1 only considers a source term from DD41 and does not consider
damage to other fuel assemblies. The staff asked an RAI to determine if an existing analysis
considers a cask drop over the spent fuel, and if that analysis bounds a potential drop of DD41
in the North Tilt Pit. The PNP UFSAR (section 14.11.3.1.1 “Radiological Consequences of a
Cask Drop in the Spent Fuel Pool”) describes what bounding analysis has been previously
performed for a cask drop in the spent fuel pool. The description in the UFSAR describes a cask
drop onto 90-day decayed fuel. In their RAI response dated October 8, 2026 (ML26281A333)
the licensee stated that calculation NAI-1149-026, Revision 0 (ML062830469) bounds a
potential drop of DD41 onto spent fuel assemblies. NAI-1149-026 postulates a cask drop which
impacts 73 fuel assemblies. The licensee stated that the FTC being used to move DD41 is not
physically large enough to impact 73 fuel assemblies. Since the analysis in NAI-1149-026
considers fuel that has a decay time significantly less than the fuel in the FTC and spent fuel
pool – and the FTC can only physically impact a number of fuel assemblies less than 73 – NAI-
                                                -8-


1149-026 can be considered a bounding analysis for moving the FTC over fuel in the spent fuel
pool.

The staff has accessed and considered the licensee-provided fuel handling procedure (FHSO-
19A) on their electronic portal to gain an understanding of both the site’s procedure and how it
aligns with the FHA analysis. The NRC staff finds that the modeling of radionuclide transport
during the analysis of an FHA is both conservative and bounding in accordance with RG 1.183,
Revision 0, and therefore acceptable.

3.2.3.1 Fuel Handling Accidents Atmospheric Dispersion values (χ/Q)

The χ/Q values used in this analysis are part of the current licensing basis and the licensee did
not request to change this aspect of its licensing basis. These values are included in the
September 25, 2006 (ML062830385), LAR Palisades - Alternative Source Term- Proposed
License Amendment.

3.2.4   Control Room (CR) Habitability for Fuel Handling Accidents

The NRC staff evaluated the applicant’s assessment of Control Room (CR) habitability following
a postulated DD41 FHA to ensure compliance with the dose limits of 10 CFR 50.67. Because
the proposed DD41 recovery process includes periods in which the fuel assembly is transported
above water and radionuclides may be released directly to containment and subsequently to the
FHB, the potential exists for atmospheric transport of radioactive material without the hold up
and retention of the reactor cavity or spent fuel pool water volume, to the control room via
normal and emergency intake pathways and including unfiltered in‑leakage. The applicant’s
analysis appropriately models both the early unfiltered intake phase and the mitigated
emergency ventilation phase, ensuring that the bounding dose to the CR operators is captured
for the duration of the event.

During the initial 20‑minute period following the postulated accident, the CR is assumed to
operate in normal ventilation mode, drawing unfiltered intake air at a rate of 660 cfm. This
assumption is conservative because it allows airborne radionuclides present in the environment
or entrained in the FHB exhaust plume to reach the CR without mitigation. The 20-minute delay
period matches the delay period which has been previously used for this analysis as
documented in Table 14.19-1 “Fuel Handling Accident (FHA) Radiological Analysis – Inputs and
Assumptions” of the PNP UFSAR. By assuming continuous unfiltered intake until operator
action, the analysis fully accounts for the most limiting period of potential CR exposure.

At 20 minutes, consistent with credited operator action and the design of the Control Room
Emergency HVAC, the control room ventilation system aligns to Emergency Mode. In this
configuration, unfiltered intake flow is terminated and replaced with filtered makeup and filtered
recirculation flows totaling approximately 1,413 cfm. A 99‑percent removal efficiency is applied
to aerosols, elemental iodine, and organic iodine species, consistent with the performance
capabilities of the emergency ventilation charcoal and HEPA filtration trains. The model also
includes 100 cfm of unfiltered in‑leakage for the duration of the accident, which conservatively
represents realistic infiltration pathways and prevents over‑crediting of CR isolation. This
treatment is consistent with NRC staff expectations for control room habitability evaluations,
particularly in analyses performed under the Alternative Source Term (AST) framework. The
applicant incorporated appropriate receptor characteristics, including a breathing rate of
3.5×10⁻⁴ m³/s and time-weighted occupancy factors of 1.0, 0.6, and 0.4 for the 0–24 hour,
                                                -9-


1–4 day, and 4-30 day periods, respectively. These values are directly aligned with RG 1.183
and NUREG‑0800 guidance for CR dose assessments.

The NRC staff audited information provided in the portal regarding the most recent Control
Room Envelope Integrated Unfiltered In-Leakage Test values. The NRC staff confirmed that the
test values did not exceed the assumed unfiltered inleakage used in the LAR. The use of higher
assumed unfiltered inleakage value provided in the LAR would result in higher calculated dose
to control room operators that is consistent with CLB, and is therefore acceptable.

Based on review of the inputs, assumptions, and the applicant’s RADTRAD modeling, the NRC
staff finds that the CR habitability assessment reasonably characterizes the range of conditions
expected following the postulated DD41 FHA. The analysis demonstrates that the total TEDE to
the control room operator remains within the 5‑rem limit of 10 CFR 50.67, even under the
bounding assumptions of early unfiltered intake, continuous infiltration, and conservative
radionuclide transport conditions. Therefore, the staff concludes that the proposed one‑time
DD41 recovery activity maintains adequate control room habitability and satisfies the guidance
of RG 1.183, Revision 0 for accident dose analyses.

Holtec evaluated the radiological consequences resulting from the postulated new variation of
an FHA and concluded that the radiological consequences at the Exclusion Area Boundary
(EAB), Low Population Zone (LPZ), and CR are within the radiological dose guidelines provided
in 10 CFR 50.67 and accident specific dose criteria specified in Standard Review Plan section
15.0.1. This evaluation is contained in the attachment for the LAR in calculation PNP 2026-052
“Radiological Consequences of DD41 FHA at Palisades.”

The NRC staff’s review found that the licensee used analysis assumptions and inputs consistent
with applicable regulatory guidance identified in the relevant sections of this safety evaluation.
The NRC staff performed an independent review of all inputs, assumptions, and initial conditions
in the licensee dose assessment files. The NRC performed confirmatory calculations using
RADTRAD version 5.2.1. The NRC staff finds that the EAB, LPZ, and CR doses for the FHA
meet the applicable accident dose criteria and are, therefore, acceptable.

3.3     Movement of Fuel Assembly DD41 Outside of the Reactor Cavity or Spent Fuel Pool

3.3.1   Radiological Source Term – 4- Year Decay

The radiological profile of DD41 after 4 years of decay and ingrowth is dominated by long-lived
fission products and transuranics. The NRC staff performed independent decay calculations,
also considering ingrowth of radionuclides due to decay to model the inventory of radionuclides
in the assembly, and compared that with the licensee modeled inventory in the assembly DD41.
The values the NRC derived using the code SCALE, were consistent with those that the
licensee calculated. The modeled assembly inventory forms the basis for understanding the
expected radiological conditions when moving the assembly in the FTC.

3.3.2   Dry Movement–Gamma and Neutron Shine in Shielded Transfer Cask

The primary radiological hazard during dry movement is external exposure (“shine”) due to
gamma and neutron decay from the unshielded assembly. Water shielding is not present, and
only cask engineering controls remain to attenuate these dose fields. The transfer cask must
                                              - 10 -


provide sufficient thickness and density to attenuate gamma and neutron emissions, maintain
shielding integrity, and prevent streaming paths.

The NRC staff performed independent confirmatory gamma-shine and neutron-shine
calculations using the SCALE code to evaluate the licensee’s assessment of external exposure
during movement of the assembly in the shielded fuel transfer canister after dewatering. The
staff’s results were consistent with those provided by the licensee and were at radiation levels
similar to those expected for comparable outage work activities. Further, the results supported
the conclusion that the transfer cask shielding is sufficient to attenuate the expected gamma
and neutron radiation fields. Based on this confirmatory analysis, the NRC staff finds that the
licensee’s evaluation of gamma-shine and neutron-shine hazards during dry movement is
acceptable.

3.3.3   Streaming and Geometry Effects

The licensee evaluated the potential for gamma streaming that could arise if a drop or other
accident involving the transfer cask were to occur as documented in section 3.2.1 “Dose
Comparisons” of the LAR. Such an event could alter shielding geometry creating localized areas
of elevated dose rate. The licensee performed analyses to assess these potential streaming
conditions. These streaming effects could be present also due to misalignment of the cask, or
any other manufacturing deviations from the drawing plans. Such an event could alter shielding
geometry. In section 3.2.1 of the LAR the licensee stated:

        The two conditions that are evaluated are normal conditions as designed, as well as
        conditions from an accidental drop of the canister that assumes a complete loss of
        neutron and gamma shielding.

This statement appeared to be contradictory to the information provided in calculation
HI-2261348, Radiological Consequences of DD41 FHA at Palisades and the document
HI-2261303 Dose Evaluation for the Fuel Transfer Canister executive summary, which state that
for a drop accident no damage to the canister is expected that would have significant impact on
dose rates and that dose rates around the canister are expected to be essentially the same as
for normal conditions. The NRC staff questioned the licensee on this item. The licensee
responded on the docket in the Response to Request for Additional Information Regarding
Emergency License Amendment Request: One-Time-Use Amendment to Allow Alternative Fuel
Handling Method for the Recovery of Fuel Assembly DD41 (ML26275A214), saying:

        A draft analysis was performed assuming total loss of neutron and gamma shielding.
        However, following the positive results from the FTC Drop Analysis contained in
        Hl-2261346, Fuel Transfer Canister Drop Analysis [], a complete loss of shielding was
        deemed not credible and subsequently removed from the radiological consequences
        analyses prior to review and approval.

The review of the FTC Drop Analysis, Hl-2261346, is covered below in section 3.4 Recovery
Equipment – Drop Analysis. The NRC staff reviewed the expected dose rates during both
normal and accident (cask drop) scenarios. The NRC staff reviewed the expected values with
the assembly in the shielded fuel transfer canister after removal from the reactor cavity as
provided in section 2.3.1 Summary of UFSAR Revised Text and 3.2.1 Dose Comparison.

The NRC staff performed independent confirmatory streaming dose-rate calculations using the
SCALE code to assess the licensee’s analysis. The staff’s results showed consistency with the
                                                - 11 -


licensee’s calculated dose rates, and the staff did not identify information that would contradict
the licensee’s conclusions with respect to streaming effects related to the FTC. The NRC staff
finds that the licensee’s evaluation provides an adequate analytical basis for characterizing
streaming-related dose rates during dry transfer.

3.3.4   Airborne Radiological Hazard

The licensee addressed the potential airborne conditions in section 3.2.3 “Airborne Radioactivity
and Contamination Controls.” Because DD41 appears to remain intact and reactor cavity
coolant sampling directly adjacent to the assembly showed no abnormal activity from fission
products, emergency ventilation actuation is not expected. In addition, the DD41 assembly’s
known structural damage and proposed handling outside the normal underwater fuel handling
configuration are addressed through the licensee’s radiation protection programs in evaluating
the potential for airborne radioactivity and contamination.

While submerged under a minimum of 20 feet of water, airborne radiological consequences
remain bounded by current licensing basis fuel handling accident radiological consequences.
Examination of the integrity of the fuel rods is vital to ensure the potential effects of airborne
contamination are minimized when the cask is removed from the reactor cavity. The cask is not
sealed, and airborne contamination is a potential risk if there is any fuel breach. To address this
issue and in response to the staff’s question, the licensee supplemented its evaluation to
include collection of a chemistry sample after the fuel assembly was placed on the FTC base
and the top of the FTC was positioned on the base. This post-movement sample will provide
additional evidence to confirm that no fuel rod damage occurred during the transition from the
assembly’s current position into the cask and thereby limit potential airborne radionuclide
concerns during the movement of the assembly and cask. In response to an RAI, the licensee
provided a calculation of the potential radiological conditions related to airborne contamination if
the fuel assembly is damaged while placing and securing the top of the FTC onto the base
holding the assembly. Based on the calculation provided, the NRC staff has reasonable
assurance that regulatory limits would not be exceed due to causing fuel failure in assembly
DD41 while securing the top of the FTC to the base. Based on the information available, the
NRC staff finds that incorporating the procedural step of examining the fuel assembly via
chemistry sample adjacent to the FTC will provide an adequate basis for verifying the
assembly’s integrity prior to movement.

3.3.5   Conclusion

Based on the information provided in the LAR and the NRC staff’s independent confirmatory
calculations, the NRC staff finds that there is reasonable assurance that the radiological
conditions during normal and accident conditions as a result of the proposed DD41 recovery
activities will not endanger the health and safety of the public and will meet the provisions of 10
CFR 20.1201, “Occupational Dose Limits for Adults,” and 10 CFR 50.67, “Accident Source
Term.”

Drop Analysis

In the application, the licensee stated that the structural response of the FTC was evaluated for
three bounding horizontal drop conditions using LSDYNA analyses that included the following:
FTC pure horizontal impact, FTC horizontal drop with the top end impacting first, and FTC
horizontal drop with the bottom end impacting first. The licensee also stated that, based on the
calculated response, the FTC maintains its overall structural configuration throughout the
evaluated impact events, all bolts have bending and shear safety factors greater than unity, and
all calculated combined-loading interaction ratios are below unity. The structural evaluation
details of the FTC drop analysis are contained in HI-2261346 Revision 0, “Fuel Transfer
Canister Drop Analysis,” which the licensee provided as part of the audit process.

The NRC staff reviewed the licensee's methodology for evaluating the structural response of the
Fuel Transfer Canister (FTC) under postulated drop conditions. The licensee developed a
detailed finite element model of the FTC and performed nonlinear dynamic analyses using LS-
DYNA to evaluate three bounding drop orientations. The analyses incorporated the FTC
geometry, material properties, structural connections, and impact conditions to determine
component stresses, strains, accelerations, and connection loads. The NRC staff finds that the
use of a nonlinear dynamic finite element analysis is an acceptable method for evaluating the
FTC response to the postulated drop events and provides an adequate basis for assessing
compliance with the established structural acceptance criteria.

The staff reviewed the results against the acceptance criteria established by the licensee, which
require that: (1) the FTC lid remain attached to the base assembly, (2) the lid-to-base bolts not
experience gross failure, (3) the end plates and shield gates remain attached to the FTC, (4) the
FTC retain and confine the fuel assembly without deformation or damage that could
compromise confinement, and (5) the FTC not experience gross structural failure that could
adversely affect shielding integrity.

The analysis results show that the FTC maintained its overall structural configuration during all
evaluated impact events. The lid and base assemblies remained engaged during impact and
rebound, calculated strains in the primary FTC components remained below the licensee's
established plastic strain limit, and the welds connecting the end plates to the lid and base
assemblies remained structurally adequate. In addition, the NRC staff verified during the audit
that the lid-to-base bolts remained structurally adequate, with safety factors greater than 1.0 and
combined loading interaction ratios less than 1.0.

Based on the analysis results, the NRC staff finds that the FTC does not experience gross
structural failure, the lid remains attached to the base assembly, the lid-to-base bolts do not
experience gross failure, and the end plates and shield gates remain attached following the
postulated drop events. The staff further finds that the FTC maintains its fuel retention,
confinement, and shielding functions. Therefore, the NRC staff concludes that the licensee has
demonstrated that the FTC satisfies the acceptance criteria for the evaluated drop accident and
will continue to perform its intended safety functions under the postulated drop conditions.

4.0    EXIGENT SITUATION

Background

The NRC's regulations contain provisions for issuance of amendments when the usual 30-day
public comment period cannot be met. These provisions are applicable under exigent
circumstances. Consistent with the requirements in 10 CFR 50.91(a)(6), exigent circumstances
exist when: (1) a licensee and the NRC must act quickly; (2) time does not permit the NRC to
publish a Federal Register notice allowing 30 days for prior public comment; and (3) the NRC
determines that the amendment involves no significant hazards consideration.

Under the provisions in 10 CFR 50.91 (a)(6), the NRC notifies the public in one of two ways: (1)
by issuing a Federal Register notice providing an opportunity for hearing and allowing at least 2
weeks from the date of the notice for prior public comments; or (2) by using local media to
provide reasonable notice to the public in the area surrounding the licensee's facility. In this
case, the NRC published notices in the Grand Rapids Press and the Kalamazoo Gazette
(October 6 and 8, 2026), and the Herald Palladium (October 7 and 8, 2026).

The licensee provided the following basis to support the finding:

       Tilting of fuel assembly DD41 was not an intended outcome of core loading and
       therefore PNP could not have foreseen the need for a license amendment to revise the
       UFSAR-described fuel-handling process and associated fuel-handling accident
                                              - 17 -


       assumptions that would support a routine licensing amendment request submission
       schedule.

       PNP is requesting emergency processing of this license amendment request as a delay
       in approval of the proposed changes would result in a delay in the resumption of
       activities necessary to reach the plant conditions required to restore the plant to power
       operation.

       10 CFR 50.91(a)(7) states “Where the Commission finds that significant hazards
       considerations are involved, it will issue a Federal Register notice providing an
       opportunity for a prior hearing even in an emergency situation, unless it finds an
       imminent danger to the health or safety of the public.” PNP concludes that the proposed
       amendment does not involve a significant hazards consideration under the standards set
       forth in 10 CFR 50.92(c), and accordingly, a finding of no significant hazards
       consideration is justified, as discussed in Section 4.2 [of the LAR].

NRC Staff Conclusion

As discussed in the licensee’s application dated September 30, 2026, the licensee requested
that the proposed amendment be processed by the NRC on an emergency basis. Although the
licensee requested that the NRC process the license amendment request under emergency
circumstances under 10 CFR 50.91(a)(5), which allows the NRC to issue a license amendment
involving no significant hazards considerations (NSHC) without prior notice and opportunity for a
hearing or for public comment, the NRC staff determined that there was sufficient time to
provide the public a reasonable opportunity for the public to comment and issue the amendment
based on exigent circumstances under 10 CFR 50.91(a)(6). The NRC staff found that it must act
quickly on the amendment request because PNP is currently loading fuel as part of its efforts to
return the plant to operation, and failure to approve the amendment in an expedited manner,
would prevent continuation of core loading activities and consequently preclude the unit’s timely
return to power operation.The NRC staff further finds that the licensee used its best efforts to
make a timely application. As stated by licensee, the tilting of fuel assembly DD41 was not an
intended outcome of core leading, so the licensee could not have foreseen the need and basis
for this amendment.

Based on these findings, and the determination that the amendment involves no significant
hazards consideration as discussed below, the NRC staff concludes that a valid need exists to
issue the license amendment under the exigent provisions of 10 CFR 50.91(a)(6).

5.0    FINAL NO SIGNIFICANT HAZARDS CONSIDERATION

Under the Atomic Energy Act of 1954, as amended, and the NRC’s regulations, the NRC staff
may issue and make an amendment immediately effective, notwithstanding the pendency
before the Commission of a request for a hearing from any person, in advance of the holding
and completion of any required hearing, where it has made a final determination that no
significant hazards consideration is involved.

The NRC’s regulation in 10 CFR 50.92(c) states that the NRC may make a final determination,
under the procedures in 10 CFR 50.91, that a license amendment involves no significant
hazards consideration if operation of the facility, in accordance with the amendment, would not:
(1) involve a significant increase in the probability or consequences of an accident previously
                                                - 18 -


evaluated; or (2) create the possibility of a new or different kind of accident from any accident
previously evaluated; or (3) involve a significant reduction in a margin of safety.

As required by 10 CFR 50.91(a), the NRC staff proposed its analysis of the issue of no
significant hazards consideration, which is presented below:

       1. Does the proposed amendment involve a significant increase in the probability or
          consequences of an accident previously evaluated?

           Response: No.

           Operation of PNP in accordance with the proposed amendment will not involve a
           significant increase in the probability or consequences of an accident previously
           evaluated. Although the DD41 proposed fuel assembly restoration path differs from
           routine fuel handling practices due to the development of the Fuel Transfer Canister
           (FTC) and lifting system, the licensee evaluated the use of the Fuel Movement
           Device (FMD) and the FTC and determined the fuel handling methods and
           administrative controls provide equivalent protection to the routine methods. There is
           no significant increase in the probability of an accident. In addition, the licensee
           evaluated the potential dose consequences of an accident during DD41 recovery
           and found there is no significant increase in the consequences of an accident as
           compared to existing safety analyses.

           The licensee's evaluation provided with the September 30, 2026, application
           documents the radiological consequences of a postulated Fuel Handling Accident
           (FHA) in accordance with Regulatory Guide 1.183, "Alternative Radiological Source
           Terms for Evaluating Designs Basis Accidents at Nuclear Power Reactors," Revision
           0 (ML003716792), pursuant to Section 50.67, "Accident source term," of Title 10 of
           the Code of Federal Regulations (10 CFR). The analysis concluded the radiological
           dose to the Control Room, Exclusion Area Boundary, and Low Population Zone
           would be within regulatory limits.

           Therefore, the proposed changes do not involve a significant increase in the
           probability or consequences of an accident previously evaluated..

       2. Does the proposed amendment create the possibility of a new or different kind of
          accident from any accident previously evaluated?

           Response: No.

           The proposed amendment will not create the possibility of a new or different kind of
           accident from any previously analyzed. An accident previously evaluated in the
           UFSAR is a fuel handling accident where a single fuel assembly is dropped during
           handling. The recovery of DD41 does not create a new or different kind of accident
           because, although the process and travel path are different from routine fuel
           handling evolutions, the overall accident progression previously evaluated remains
           the same. The proposed activity does not introduce potential damage to more than a
           single fuel assembly, and the accident remains bound by the existing FHA described
           in UFSAR Section 14.19.

           Similarly, the loaded FTC movements within the fuel handling building follow
                                               - 19 -


           previously approved designated safe load paths using a single failure proof crane.

           The fuel handling activity was evaluated for the use of a FTC to move DD41 in a dry
           condition. The evaluation determined that moving the fuel dry did not create the
           possibility of a new or different kind of accident, and the accident scenario remains
           bounded by the existing UFSAR Section 14.19 FHA.

           Therefore, the proposed changes do not create the possibility of a new or different
           kind of accident from any previously evaluated.

       3. Does the proposed amendment involve a significant reduction in a margin of safety?

           Response: No.

           The proposed amendment will not involve a significant reduction in a margin of
           safety. Margin of safety is associated with confidence in the ability of the fission
           product barriers (i.e., fuel cladding, reactor coolant system pressure boundary, and
           containment structure) to limit the level of radiation dose to the public. The proposed
           amendment would modify the PNP licensing basis to allow for a one-time use fuel
           handling activity for recovery of DD41. A postulated accident involving DD41 remains
           bounded by the UFSAR Section 14.19 FHA analysis of record.

           Based on results of the thermal and fuel oxidation evaluations, the analyzed fuel
           transfer operation maintains the fuel cladding temperature below the applicable limit
           and restricts uranium dioxide oxidation to acceptable levels that maintain fuel
           cladding integrity during the recovery of DD41.

           There will be no effect on plant systems necessary to perform protection functions.
           No instrument setpoints or system response times are affected and none of the
           acceptance criteria for any accident analysis will be changed. Consequently, the
           proposed change will have no impact on the radiological consequences of a design
           basis accident.

           Therefore, the proposed changes do not involve a significant reduction in a margin of
           safety.

The NRC staff reviewed the licensee’s no significant hazards consideration determination.
Based on this review, and the staff’s evaluation of the underlying LAR, as discussed above, the
NRC staff concludes that the three standards of 10 CFR 50.92(c) are satisfied. Therefore, the
NRC staff has made a final determination that no significant hazards consideration is involved
for the proposed amendment and that the amendment should be issued as allowed by the
criteria contained in 10 CFR 50.91.

provide reasonable notice to the public to provide comments in the area surrounding the
licensee's facility. In this case, the NRC published notices in the Grand Rapids Press and the
Kalamazoo Gazette (October 6 and 8, 2026), and the Herald Palladium (October 7 and 8,

8.0    ENVIRONMENTAL CONSIDERATION

This action relates to authorizations under 10 CFR Part 50 with respect to installation or use of a
facility component. The NRC staff has determined that any ground disturbance is limited to
previously disturbed areas. Additionally, the NRC staff has determined that the action involves
no significant change in the types or significant increase in the amounts of any effluents that
may be released offsite, no significant increase in individual or cumulative public or occupational
radiation exposure, and no significant increase in the potential for or consequences from
radiological accidents. Finally, the NRC staff has determined that a categorical exclusion applies
and that special circumstances under 10 CFR 51.22, “Categorical exclusions,” are not present
that would preclude reliance on the categorical exclusion. Accordingly, this action meets the
eligibility criteria for categorical exclusion set forth in 10 CFR 51.22(d)(8). Pursuant to
10 CFR 51.22, no environmental impact statement or environmental assessment need be
prepared for this action in connection with the action.

9.0    CONCLUSION

The Commission has concluded, based on the considerations discussed above, that: (1) there

conducted in compliance with the Commission’s regulations, and (3) the issuance of the
amendment will not be inimical to the common defense and security or to the health and safety
of the public.
